title: Impact of vaccination and preterm delivery on maternal RSV-specific peripheral and mucosal immunity
text:
In the United States and globally, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality
in infants under 6 months, with preterm infants at particularly high risk of severe disease. A bivalent RSV vaccine
recently licensed for use in pregnancy provides ~70% protection from severe RSV disease in infants; the vaccine
boosts maternal and cord IgG, however, the impact on breastmilk immunity is unknown. The proposed work will
carefully dissect the impact of maternal RSV vaccine on both peripheral and breastmilk immunity in term and
preterm dyads, empowering the development of next generation maternal vaccines to improve infant protection.

title: Targeting Lag-3 and PD -1 in Myeloid Cells of GBM
text:
Checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy has improved the treatment of many solid tumors,
and an active investigation to treat glioblastomas (GBM) with a dual immune checkpoint
blockade strategy has thus far yielded promising signs of efficacy. Our proposal aims to
study the mechanisms by which immune checkpoint blockades promote a multifaceted
immune response in GBM tumor types. A thorough understanding of these mechanisms
will further inform the effective design of new strategies, and improve current therapeutic
strategies, for patients with GBM.

title: Pen-and-Paper and Smartphone Self-Reported Cognitive Concerns to Predict Longitudinal Alzheimer's Biomarkers in a Diverse, Non-Demented Older Adult Population
text:
This project aims to improve early detection of Alzheimer’s Disease and related dementias
(ADRD) by focusing on self-reported cognitive concerns (SCC) as an accessible and cost-
effective screening tool. It will compare traditional pen-and-paper assessments with
smartphone-based methods and use machine learning to integrate both approaches for
predicting AD plasma biomarkers, which reflect disease risk. The study will also explore how
these methods perform across different racial and ethnic groups, advancing health equity in
ADRD research.

title: Embryonic Cell Recognition: Specificity Determinants
text:
An epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) occurs in almost all animals, moving cells that originate in an
epithelium to produce the connective tissue of the embryo. In embryos this process must be completed, and
in carcinomas the EMT process is co-opted and must be stopped. Thus, in order to prevent birth defects, and
to stop metastatic events it is crucial to understand how the EMT works, which is the goal of this project.

title: Deciphering fungal pathogen-specific cell cycle mechanisms to fuel drug discovery
text:
Fungal infections are a pressing and underappreciated threat to global public health, yet treatment options are
limited due to the cellular similarities between fungi and humans. Using an important human fungal pathogen
Cryptococcus neoformans as a model system, this proposal aims to dissect fungal-specific cell cycle variations
that are essential for C. neoformans’s ability to proliferate and evade the host immune system during infection.
Results from this work will uncover unique aspects of fungal pathogen biology and facilitate the identification of
new targets for antifungal development.

title: Assessing the longitudinal impact of Mediterranean diet interventions to reduce cognitive decline on gut microbiota composition and bile acid variety
text:
Alzheimer's disease affects millions and its prevalence is expected to rise, posing a significant public health
challenge and motivating preventive lifestyle interventions. This proposal aims to explore how the
Mediterranean diet influences gut microbiome and metabolome composition to mitigate cognitive decline. The
results will enhance our understanding of dietary impacts on brain health and reveal diagnostic and therapeutic
targets to ease the burden of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias on our aging population.

title: Somatic Repeat Expansions as a Therapeutic Target for Trinucleotide Repeat Disorders
text:
Repeat expansions disorders such as Huntington’s Disease and Friedreich Ataxia are severely debilitating
rare neurodegenerative disorders, for which, despite the underlying genetic mutations being known for over 20
years now, there are still no effective therapies available, suggesting that novel approaches are necessary. There
is growing evidence that somatic repeat expansion is a shared hallmark across the different repeat expansion
disorders and that this may contribute to disease onset and progression, supporting further investigation of
repeat expansion mechanism(s) as potential therapeutic targets. This study is aimed at: 1) identification of non-
invasive samples that can be used as potential biomarkers of disease; 2) development of novel methodology to
better size and quantify repeat instability; 3) discovery and characterization of genetic modifiers of somatic repeat
expansions, 4) development of novel therapeutics targeting the repeat expansion process as a potential
universal treatment for these devastating disorders.

title: Studying the initiation, progression and therapy of lung cancer in mouse models
text:
Lung cancer is a global scourge responsible for 1.5 million patient deaths worldwide, and ~130,000
patient deaths in the USA this year alone. Despite these grim statistics, lung cancer treatment has
been revolutionized by the fundamental scientific understanding that lung cancers can be genetically
subdivided based on the presence of specific proto-oncogene mutations that, in turn, predict for
responsiveness to FDA-approved pathway-targeted therapies. Here, we propose the use of
experimental/preclinical models of KRAS- or BRAF-driven lung cancer in combination with inhibitors of
cellular signaling pathways to define the importance of key pathways in lung cancer initiation,
progression and therapy, with the overarching goal of developing a rational scientific foundation for the
development of new combination therapy strategies to more effectively treat lung cancer patients.

title: Development of porcine stem cell-based technologies to improve the efficiency, reliability, and reproducibility of animal models
text:
Genetically engineered pigs are important for studying human diseases, testing new treatments, and helping
solve the shortage of organs for transplant, to name a few. However, current methods for creating these
special pigs are slow and unreliable. This project will improve how we modify pig genes using stem cells,
making it faster and more accurate to create models of human disease and transplantation research, ultimately
helping to develop better medical treatments.

title: Gene Expression in Long-Term Memory
text:
This project will employ state-of-the-art molecular, biochemical, and genetic techniques in mice to identify the
cell types and mechanisms that regulate and functionally recruit the IGF-2/IGF-2R system in the hippocampus
to form long-term memory. It will test the hypotheses that IGF-2 released by specific cell types, such as pericytes,
activates IGF-2R expressed by target cells, such as neurons, to regulate, via vesicle trafficking, de novo
translation induced by learning and its coupling to autophagy, a fundamental molecular node that controls
plasticity changes essential for memory formation. Targeting this novel mechanism should provide important
insights for treating disorders associated to memory impairment.

title: CRCNS: A computational approach to map visual cortex organization in the human brain
text: Neuroscientists have made strides in understanding the visual cortex's organization, but accurately identifying its components in individuals remains challenging, hampering both scientific and clinical progress. Here, we develop machine learning tools to accurately delineate the multiple visual brain regions in individual human subjects and then model how these regions vary and covary across people. The results will greatly increase the ability of basic scientists and clinicians to study the many separate parts of the cortical visual system in humans, furthering neuroscientific understanding of vision and links between cortical organization and visual health.

title: Glutamatergic plasticity that drives cannabinoid withdrawal and craving
text:
Initiation of cannabis use usually occurs during adolescence, which represents a vulnerable period in
neurobiological development. The proposed research is designed to elucidate how chronic cannabinoid use
during adolescence produces neural plasticity- that is changes in brain structure and function- related to short-
and long-term behavioral adaptations exemplified by withdrawal and relapse-like behavior. Identifying these
important adaptations may inform the development of novel therapies for cannabis use disorder.

title: Hub4Smell: Advancing Human Olfactory Research through Digital Innovation and Community Engagement
text:
Millions of people are experiencing smell dysfunction, which has a profound, unrecognized impact on health
and economics. Lack of routine smell testing impairs research and clinical care in human olfaction. To advance
human olfactory research and care we address these issues by launching and validating Hub4Smell, a
collaborative digital platform that centralizes human olfactory data from various tests and users, provides
insights through a generative AI exploratory module and grants access to expert knowledge, ultimately
facilitating the adoption of smell testing in research and clinical settings.

title: Cellular Innovation via Organelle Theft
text:
My research program seeks to elucidate the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying organelle theft, a
rare but remarkable biological phenomenon whereby animals sequester functional organelles from other
species, thereby acquiring novel traits and capabilities. Leveraging these unique organisms as models, we
investigate organelle theft as a fundamental cellular principle that has been largely overlooked, employing a
comparative and multidisciplinary approach across diverse lineages, including the sequestration of chloroplasts
by sacoglossan sea slugs and stinging organelles by nudibranch slugs. Through this work, we aim to uncover
core principles of organelle acquisition, maintenance, and integration that hold broad implications for
understanding symbiosis, cellular evolution, and potential biomedical innovation.

title: Core C:  Uganda
text:
Modified Public Health Relevance Section. 
 
The Uganda Core C will provide access to samples from sub-Saharan Africa, which remains an epicenter for the HIV pandemic. The advanced research performed on Ugandan samples by the CFAR in the US offers an opportunity to effectively train multiple Ugandan investigators during visits to the USA and launch their careers as future leaders in the HIV/AIDS field.

title: Adenine Base Edited Correction of Cystic Fibrosis Airways
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because genetic and acquired diseases affecting the
airways pose major disease and economic burdens. Small molecule CFTR potentiators or correctors have
provided groundbreaking improvements in the quality of life for most people with CF; however, these drug
treatments are not cures and provide no benefit to the ~10% of CF patients with nonsense CFTR mutations.
Unlike small molecule potentiators or correctors, a CFTR gene editing approach is potentially a single dose,
life-long curative therapeutic strategy for many people with CF.

title: BCM/RICE GENOME EDITING TESTING CENTER
text:
Genome editing systems have the potential to cure some of the most severe human diseases. However, there
are significant efficacy and safety issues that must be addressed before this technology can be applied in clinical
trials. The BCM/Rice Genome Editing Testing Center will provide mouse resources and testing fee-for-services
to the growing community developing new genome editing technologies and conducting preclinical testing based
upon these technologies.

title: Developing Novel Deep-Learning Based Methods for Deciphering Non-Coding Gene Regulatory Code
text:
The disruption of numerous human genes and their isoforms driven by germline and somatic variants is
implicated in various cancers. This project will contribute DNABERT, a genomic large language model, based
deep-learning approaches that will result in transformative genome foundation models and predictive algorithms
for integrative analyses of multi-omics datasets. The proposed algorithms will enable identification of combination
of genetic variants that alter the gene regulatory landscape, gene expression and cellular composition, leading
to tissue-type specific developmental risk mechanisms for brain, lung and colorectal cancers.

title: Biospeciman Analysis Core
text: Biospecimen Analysis Core The Biospecimen Analysis Core will drive the development of virome data from samples acquired by the Biospecimen Collection Core of the Penn VCC. The Biospecimen Analysis Core will be led by Dr. Frederic Bushman at Penn and Dr. Ahmed Moustafa at CHOP, together with co-I Dr. Gary Wu. All have published multiple papers together, and work together closely in managing the PennCHOP Microbiome Program. The Biospecimen Analysis Core will work closely with the Penn VCC Biospecimen Collection Core to analyze samples collected from multiple body sites of children and adults, emphasizing joint analysis of oral, respiratory, gut and blood specimens. The approach will combine biobanked samples from existing cohorts with prospective resampling from many of the same individuals, allowing very long term longitudinal assessment. The Penn VCC has samples in hand for analysis over the first two years of the program, enabling immediate startup and data generation, and will turn to newly collected samples in years 3-5. The Biospecimen Analysis Core will carry out sequence analysis of purified virome specimens, and also metagenomic analysis of specimens by both whole genome shotgun sequencing and in selected low biomass samples also 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The Biospecimen Analysis Core will also carry out long read single molecule sequencing, including analyzing phage covalent DNA modification, and HiC to assign phages to hosts. The Core will also lead exploratory imaging studies. Thus we will address a wealth of questions on the nature and function of the human virome, while advancing the goals of the full HVP. The overall approach of the Biospecimen Analysis Core will be to: Aim 1. Optimize methods and validate procedures for sequence-based analysis of the virome and the background host microbiome. Aim 2. Generate sequence data on the virome and the full microbiome. Aim 3. Explore potential insights from additional methods including long read single molecule sequencing, HiC, imaging and others.

title: VisualSonics Vevo F2 LAZR-X20 Photoacoustic and Ultrasound Imaging System
text:
The VisualSonics Vevo F2 LAZR-X20 requested in this proposal is a uniquely integrated ultrasound and
photoacoustic imaging system specifically designed for non-invasive pre-clinical small and large animal imaging.
The equipment will be used by several users, all of which have varying levels of experience working with
photoacoustic/ultrasound imaging systems and are experts in their own respective fields including cancer
research, cardiovascular research, neurobiology, infectious diseases, and optical engineering. At the Wellman
Center for Photomedicine and Massachusetts General Hospital, the Vevo F2 LAZR-X20 system will complement
current imaging technologies and transcend some of their limitations.
